basis.ref: Expected return and volatility with scenarios · Folien 12–13

prompt: Stock X returns 25% in a boom (probability 0.3), 10% in a normal year (0.5) and −15% in a recession (0.2). Compute its expected return and its volatility. Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Expected return
steps.why: Weight each return with its probability and add up.

steps.title: Squared deviations from the expected return
steps.why: Deviation = scenario return − 9.5 (in percentage points), then square it.

steps.title: Variance
steps.why: With scenarios (probabilities) you weight the squared deviations by the probabilities – there is no T − 1 here.

pitfalls: Dividing by n − 1 – that rule is only for historical data, not for scenarios with probabilities.
Forgetting to take the square root (reporting the variance).

basis.ref: Worked example: two stocks, four years · Folien 45–47

prompt: (a) Compute the average return and the volatility of each stock. Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Average returns
steps.why: Add the four yearly returns and divide by 4.

steps.title: Deviations from the mean (in percentage points)
Variance and volatility of A
steps.why: Historical data → divide the sum of squares by T − 1 = 3.

pitfalls: Dividing by 4 instead of 3 for historical data.

basis.ref: Worked example: covariance, correlation, beta · Folien 48–49

prompt: (b) Compute the covariance and the correlation between A and B, and the beta of B with respect to A. Give the covariance in decimals (e.g. 0.0012).

steps.title: Deviations from part (a)
steps.why: Use the same deviations as before (in percentage points): A − 6% and B − 4%.

steps.title: Covariance
steps.why: Historical data → divide the sum of products by T − 1 = 3.

steps.title: Correlation
steps.why: Correlation = covariance divided by both volatilities. It always lies between −1 and +1.

steps.title: Beta of B with respect to A
steps.why: Beta = covariance divided by the variance of the reference asset (here A).

pitfalls: Dividing the covariance by Var(B) – the beta "of B on A" uses the variance of A.
Mixing units: keep everything in decimals (0.0016, 0.004533), not percent.

prompt: (c) What are the expected return and the volatility of a portfolio invested 50% in A and 50% in B? Compare with the volatilities of A and B alone. Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
E(Rp) = 0.5 × 6.00% + 0.5 × 4.00% = 5.00%.
Var(Rp) = 0.25 × 0.004533 + 0.25 × 0.001467 + 2 × 0.25 × (-0.0016) = 0.000700.
σp = 2.65% – far below 6.73% and 3.83%: the negative covariance makes risks cancel (check: portfolio returns 8.5%, 2.5%, 3.5%, 5.5% give the same variance).

steps.title: Expected return of the portfolio
steps.why: The portfolio return is the weighted average of the returns.

steps.title: Portfolio variance
steps.why: Var(Rp) = xA² Var(A) + xB² Var(B) + 2 xA xB Cov(A,B)

steps.title: Compare
steps.why: A alone: 6.73%, B alone: 3.83%, the mix: only 2.65%. The negative covariance means that A tends to be high when B is low, so the risks cancel out.
lines: Check: portfolio returns per year 8.5%, 2.5%, 3.5%, 5.5% → same σ = 2.65%

pitfalls: Taking the weighted average of the volatilities (5.28%) – that ignores the covariance.
Forgetting the factor 2 in front of the covariance term.

basis.ref: Risk of a portfolio with two stocks · Folie 39

prompt: You invest EUR 3,000 in stock A (expected return 6%, volatility 20%) and EUR 1,000 in stock B (expected return 16%, volatility 40%). The correlation is 0.3. What are the expected return and the volatility of your portfolio? Report percentages with two decimals.

steps.title: Portfolio weights
steps.why: Weight = amount in the stock / total amount invested.

steps.title: Portfolio variance – term by term
steps.why: Var = xA² σA² + xB² σB² + 2 xA xB ρ σA σB

pitfalls: Using amounts (3,000 / 1,000) instead of weights in the formula.
Using the correlation instead of the covariance: the cross term needs ρ × σA × σB.

prompt: You have EUR 10,000. You short-sell EUR 4,000 of stock B and invest EUR 14,000 in stock A. A: expected return 10%, volatility 20%. B: expected return 6%, volatility 15%. Correlation 0.3. What are the portfolio weights, the expected return and the volatility? Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
Weights are computed on your own money: xA = 14,000/10,000 = 1.4, xB = −4,000/10,000 = −0.4 (sum = 1).
E(Rp) = 1.4 × 10% − 0.4 × 6% = 11.60%.
Var = 1.4² × 0.04 + 0.4² × 0.0225 + 2 × 1.4 × (−0.4) × 0.3 × 0.20 × 0.15 = 0.0784 + 0.0036 − 0.01008 = 0.07192.
σp = 26.82%. The short position flips the sign of the cross term, the squared weight still adds risk.

steps.title: Portfolio weights on your own money
steps.why: Weights are always measured relative to your own capital (EUR 10,000). A short position gets a negative weight. The weights still add up to 1.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: Squared weights are always positive, so the short position still adds its own risk. Only the cross term changes sign.

pitfalls: Using 14,000/18,000 as weights – the base is your own money, not the gross position.

prompt: An investor has mean–variance utility U = E(R) − (γ/2) × Var(R) with γ = 3. Investment 1 offers 8% expected return with 10% volatility, investment 2 offers 12% with 25%. Compute both utilities (in %) and say which the investor prefers.
modelAnswer:
U₁ = 0.08 − 1.5 × 0.10² = 0.08 − 0.015 = 6.50%.
U₂ = 0.12 − 1.5 × 0.25² = 0.12 − 0.09375 = 2.62%.
The investor prefers investment 1: the extra 4% of return does not compensate a risk-averse investor (γ = 3) for the much higher variance.

steps.title: The formula
steps.why: U = E(R) − (γ/2) × Var(R). With γ = 3 the penalty is 1.5 × variance. Use decimals!

steps.title: Decision
steps.why: The investor chooses the higher utility: investment 1. Investment 2 offers 4 percentage points more return, but the risk penalty is more than 6 percentage points higher.

pitfalls: Using the volatility instead of the variance in the penalty.
Calculating in percent (8 − 1.5 × 10²) – the formula only works in decimals.

basis.ref: The three monsters: covariance, correlation, beta · Folien 31–34

prompt: The covariance between the returns of stocks A and B is 0.012. A has a volatility of 20%, B of 30%. Compute the correlation and the beta of A with respect to B.
modelAnswer:
ρ = Cov/(σA σB) = 0.012/(0.20 × 0.30) = 0.012/0.06 = 0.20.
β(A on B) = Cov/Var(B) = 0.012/0.30² = 0.012/0.09 = 0.1333.
All three measures use the covariance; they only differ in what you divide by.

steps.title: Correlation
steps.why: Correlation = covariance divided by the product of both volatilities.

steps.title: Beta of A with respect to B
steps.why: Beta = covariance divided by the variance of the reference asset B.

steps.title: Note
steps.why: All three measures start from the covariance; they only differ in what you divide by.

pitfalls: Dividing by σB (0.30) instead of the variance σB² (0.09) for the beta.

prompt: A portfolio invests 60% in stock A (volatility 20%) and 40% in stock B (volatility 30%). Compute the portfolio volatility if the correlation is (a) +1 and (b) 0. Report percentages with two decimals.
modelAnswer:
(a) ρ = +1: no diversification, σp = 0.6 × 20% + 0.4 × 30% = 24.00%.
(b) ρ = 0: Var = 0.36 × 0.04 + 0.16 × 0.09 = 0.0144 + 0.0144 = 0.0288 → σp = 16.97%.
With ρ < 1 the portfolio risk lies below the weighted average – that is diversification.

steps.title: The general formula
lines: σp² = xA² σA² + xB² σB² + 2 xA xB ρ σA σB

steps.title: (a) ρ = +1: no diversification
steps.why: With perfect correlation the formula becomes a perfect square, so the volatility is just the weighted average.

steps.title: Interpretation
steps.why: Whenever ρ < 1, the portfolio volatility lies below the weighted average of the volatilities – that is diversification.

pitfalls: Using the weighted average of volatilities when ρ ≠ 1.

basis.ref: Volatility of a portfolio of N stocks · Folie 41

prompt: Which part of a stock's risk disappears in a well-diversified portfolio, and which part does not? Explain using the variance of an equally weighted portfolio of N stocks.
modelAnswer: Idiosyncratic (firm-specific) risk disappears: firm-specific news is independent across firms and averages out. Systematic (market) risk remains, because all firms are exposed to common factors (economy, interest rates). In an equally weighted portfolio Var = (1/N) × average variance + (1 − 1/N) × average covariance. As N grows, the own-variance term goes to zero and the variance converges to the average covariance – the systematic risk that cannot be diversified away.
keyPoints: Idiosyncratic / firm-specific risk is diversified away
Portfolio risk converges to the average covariance
